author: George Bernard Shaw
parts: The great secret, Eliza,
is not having bad manners or good manners
or any other particular sort of manners,
but having the same manner for all human souls:
hints: A professor of speech bets he can pass off a flower seller as a duchess
note: Higgins defends being rude to everyone equally. Shaw refused to let the play end with a wedding, and wrote an essay explaining why.

work: Loveliest of trees, the cherry now
author: A. E. Housman
parts: Loveliest of trees,
the cherry now / Is hung with bloom along the bough,
/ And stands about the woodland ride
/ Wearing white for Eastertide.
hints: A man of twenty works out he has only fifty springs left to see the blossom
note: Poem II of A Shropshire Lad. Easter falls on 28 March in 2027, two days after this line.

author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
parts: In the Spring
a young man's fancy
lightly turns
to thoughts of love.
hints: A young man returns to the house by the sea where his cousin turned him down
note: Quoted as if it's cheerful. In the poem the speaker is bitter: the cousin he loved married a richer man.

author: Robert Browning
parts: Oh, to be in England
/ Now that April's there,
/ And whoever wakes in England
/ Sees, some morning, unaware,
hints: An Englishman in Italy is homesick for elm leaves, chaffinches and buttercups
note: Browning wrote it in Italy, where he later lived with Elizabeth Barrett Browning (day 89). The poem ends by preferring buttercups to Italian flowers.

author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
parts: Nothing is so beautiful as Spring—
/ When weeds, in wheels,
shoot long and lovely and lush;
/ Thrush's eggs look little low heavens,
hints: A sonnet written in the 1870s, printed in 1918
A priest-poet sees thrushes' eggs and racing lambs as a glimpse of Eden
note: Hopkins, a Jesuit, never published his poems. His friend Robert Bridges printed them in 1918, nearly thirty years after his death.

work: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
author: Thomas Gray
parts: The boast of heraldry, the pomp of pow'r,
/ And all that beauty, all that wealth e'er gave,
/ Awaits alike th' inevitable hour.
/ The paths of glory lead but to the grave.
hints: At dusk in a village churchyard, a poet thinks about the poor buried there
note: General Wolfe is said to have recited the poem the night before he died taking Quebec, saying he'd rather have written it.

search.title: elegy written in a country churchyard
search.creator: gray

author: Langston Hughes
parts: I've known rivers:
/ I've known rivers ancient as the world
and older than the flow of human blood in human veins.
/ My soul has grown deep like the rivers.
hints: A speaker remembers the Euphrates, the Congo, the Nile and the Mississippi
note: Hughes wrote it at about 18 on a train crossing the Mississippi. It was printed in The Crisis in June 1921.

author: Matthew Arnold
parts: The sea is calm to-night.
/ The tide is full,
the moon lies fair
/ Upon the straits;
hints: A man at a window above the Channel hears faith ebbing like the tide
note: The calm doesn't last. By the end the world has "neither joy, nor love, nor light", and the only comfort left is being true to each other.

author: John Masefield
parts: I must down to the seas again,
to the lonely sea and the sky,
/ And all I ask is a tall ship
and a star to steer her by,
hints: A former sailor longs for the wind, the gulls and a merry yarn
note: Masefield went to sea at fifteen and later became Poet Laureate. Early printings say "I must down"; the "go" most people add came later.

author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
parts: Sunset and evening star,
/ And one clear call for me!
/ And may there be no moaning of the bar,
/ When I put out to sea,
hints: An old poet imagines his death as a ship leaving harbour
note: The bar is a sandbank at a harbour mouth. Tennyson asked that this poem be printed last in every collection of his work.

author: Lord Byron
parts: Roll on,
thou deep and dark blue Ocean—roll!
/ Ten thousand fleets sweep over thee in vain;
/ Man marks the earth with ruin—his control / Stops with the shore;
hints: A long poem whose last part came out in the 1810s
A gloomy young nobleman travels through Europe
note: From the last canto. The poem made Byron famous overnight; he said he woke one morning to find himself so.

author: Daniel Defoe
parts: It happened one day, about noon, going towards my boat,
I was exceedingly surprised
with the print of a man's naked foot on the shore,
which was very plain to be seen in the sand.
hints: A castaway spends twenty-eight years on an island
note: Crusoe has been alone for fifteen years. One footprint terrifies him more than the shipwreck did. ("In the sand" is the 1719 first edition; some modern texts print "on".)

author: J. M. Synge
parts: They're all gone now,
and there isn't anything more
the sea
can do to me.
hints: An old woman on the Aran Islands loses the last of her sons
note: Maurya has lost her husband and six sons to the sea. Synge heard the islanders' English on his visits to Aran and wrote it down.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson
parts: This be the verse you grave for me:
/ Here he lies where he longed to be;
/ Home is the sailor, home from sea,
/ And the hunter home from the hill.
hints: A writer composes his own epitaph
note: The lines are on Stevenson's grave on a mountain in Samoa. People often say "home from the sea"; he wrote "home from sea".

author: Mark Twain
parts: Work consists of whatever
a body is obliged to do,
and that Play consists of whatever
a body is not obliged to do.
hints: A boy on the Mississippi tricks his friends into whitewashing a fence
note: The moral Tom would have learned from the fence, "if he had been a great and wise philosopher". His friends paid him for the chance to paint it.

author: Rupert Brooke
parts: If I should die, think only this of me:
/ That there's some corner of a foreign field
/ That is for ever
/ England.
hints: A young man going to war imagines his grave abroad
note: Brooke died of an infected mosquito bite on the way to Gallipoli in April 1915, months after the sonnet was first printed. He is buried on the Greek island of Skyros.

author: W. B. Yeats
parts: I will arise and go now,
and go to Innisfree,
/ And a small cabin build there,
of clay and wattles made:
hints: On a grey London pavement a man dreams of an island with bean rows and a beehive
note: Yeats said a fountain in a London shop window, with a little ball balanced on its jet, set off the memory of a lake in Sligo.

author: L. M. Montgomery
parts: isn't it nice to think
that to-morrow is a new day
with no mistakes
in it yet?
hints: An orphan girl with red hair is sent by mistake to a brother and sister on Prince Edward Island
note: Anne says it after a day of disasters. Montgomery built the book from a note she had made years earlier: a couple ask for a boy and are sent a girl. ("To-morrow" is the 1908 first edition's spelling.)

work: The Fall of the House of Usher
author: Edgar Allan Poe
parts: During the whole of a dull, dark, and soundless day
in the autumn of the year,
when the clouds hung oppressively low in the heavens,
I had been passing alone, on horseback,
through a singularly dreary tract of country;
hints: A visitor arrives at a crumbling house where a brother and sister are the last of their line
note: Poe wanted every word of a story to build one effect. Here the sentence itself is long, low and heavy, like the clouds.

author: Voltaire
who: Candide (anonymous translation, London: George Redway, 1898; reprinted New York: Boni and Liveright, 1918)
parts: “All that is very well,”
answered Candide,
“but let us cultivate
our garden.”
hints: A French satire from the 1750s, in translation
A young man taught that all is for the best meets war, earthquake and the Inquisition
note: The book's last words. Pangloss is still insisting that everything happened for the best; Candide stops arguing and goes back to work.
reserve_reason: The famous wording ("let us cultivate our garden") comes from an anonymous translation; Smollett's named one has "take care of our garden". Swapped out because every translation must name its translator.
